title: Who Else Is Standing Here
segs: Chapter 4. Who Else Is Standing Here.

On Thursday, Anaya took her proof to Lakshmi Iyer. Lakshmi is Sahaj's head of compliance. Her job is to make sure the company follows the rules. She had spent twenty years in a bank. She read the printout, the thirty-seven flags and the numbered notes. She read like a person who has been fooled by papers before. She looked for what had been left out.
She saw that the nine percent came from one week and one chatbot. Anaya said the notes already said that. "That is the only reason I am still reading," said Lakshmi.

Anaya told her what she wanted to build. The tool would spot identity numbers and other personal details in a message. It would hide them before the message went anywhere else. The cleaned messages would still go to an outside company. Its software (the program that writes the chatbot's replies) belongs to that company.

Lakshmi said a "yes, but". She would not stop a tool that made Sahaj hold less data. She would stop a tool that sent more data out. If the cleaning happened inside the company, before anything left, she could accept it. If it happened on someone else's computer, she could not.
She asked one more question. How would Anaya know the tool worked? Anaya did not know yet. Lakshmi told her to come back when she did.

This chapter follows the work that came next. Anaya checks if the tool already exists. She measures how big the chance is. She studies the other choices. Then she turns her notes from the talks into a ranked list.
The case: a yes, but.
It is like a shopkeeper who says, "You may open here, but only on my side of the road." The "yes, but" did two things.
First, it settled the riskiest guess from the last chapter. Sahaj could pass cleaned text to an outside company, if one condition was met.

Second, it fixed a rule for the design before any design existed. The tool had to run on Sahaj's side of the wall. That ruled out many easy designs. It ruled out every service that takes the raw message in order to clean it.
An early rule like this is a gift. It removes options for free, while they are still ideas and no work has been spent on them.
Has someone already done this?

Next came a question Anaya should have asked weeks earlier. What if the tool already exists? Think of it as checking the shop in the next lane before you open a new one. She spent one evening looking.

She found an open tool called Rampart. Open means anyone can use and read it. It was free. Capable people had built and tested it. Its job was exactly what she had in mind: find personal details in text. Its makers had published an honest list. The list said which languages they had tested, and how well the tool did. It covered English and six European languages. All of them use the Latin alphabet, the A to Z letters.

She read the part on Hindi twice. By its own results, the tool found only about fourteen in every hundred personal details in Hindi. That was Hindi written in the Devanagari script, the Hindi letters.

She wrote the number down with a question mark. Her rule about claims worked both ways. It applied to claims she liked, as well as claims she did not. She would check it herself later. Even unchecked, the number showed where the tool's reach ended.

Sahaj's customers did not stay inside that edge. They wrote in English. They wrote in Hindi. They also wrote in the form Sanjay Patil had shown her without meaning to. That is Hindi spelled in English letters, mixed with English words, often in one sentence. A tool built for one way of writing would meet three.
Sizing the opportunity.
Next Anaya asked who would want the tool. She answered with numbers. There are two ways to guess the size of a market. A market is all the people who might buy.

The first way starts from an industry report. It sounds like this: "Customer-support software is a ten-billion-dollar market, so if we win one percent...". It is quick, and almost useless. Nobody can say how the one percent would be won.

The second way starts from customers you can count, and adds upwards. It is like counting the shops in your own lane, and then adding up what each will pay. This is a bottom-up estimate (a size built from the ground up). Its great strength is that every guess sits on the page. Anyone can question it.

She began with the biggest group she could defend. That was registered lenders and finance apps in India. A public list held about nine thousand names. That was a fact. Then she guessed that a small firm might pay about ₹1.2 lakh a year for such a tool. That was a guess, and she marked it as one.
From here, three sizes come up again and again, one inside the next. Here are their names.
Definition: Three sizes, one inside the next.

Think of every shop in a city. The total addressable market (TAM) is everyone who has the problem, at the price you would charge. The serviceable addressable market (SAM) is the part of the TAM you could serve with what you have. It is the shops in your part of the city. The serviceable obtainable market (SOM) is the part of the SAM you could really win in about three years.
The table shows Anaya's numbers. Each row is smaller than the row above it.

Table 4.1: Anaya's bottom-up estimate for the privacy tool. TAM. What it means: Everyone who has the problem. Calculation: 9,000 firms × ₹1.2 lakh = about ₹108 crore a year. SAM. What it means: The part she could serve. Calculation: 2,700 firms that run a chat and handle 5,000 chats a month or more = about ₹32 crore. SOM. What it means: What she could win in about three years. Calculation: 2 percent of 2,700 = 54 customers = about ₹65 lakh a year.
The last number made her stop and think. ₹65 lakh a year pays for a small team. It does not make a company. But she could believe it. She could not say that about the first number.

She built the estimate in a spreadsheet, not on paper. A spreadsheet is a grid of boxes that does sums for you. Each number sat in its own box (a cell). Each total was a formula, a sum that points at those boxes. Farah questioned the price per customer. Anaya changed one cell, and every total below it changed too. An estimate that updates itself invites argument. That is what an estimate is for.

The final number was not the point of the table. Every line raised a question. How did she know there were nine thousand firms, or five thousand chats? And every question had somewhere to go. Each number was marked as known or guessed. The guessed ones were the first to be checked.
Competition in three kinds.

Most people think of rivals as a list of other products. Anaya sorted hers into three kinds. It is like asking how a family could get a hot meal. They could order from a rival restaurant. They could use a tiffin service. Or they could keep cooking at home, as they always do.

Table 4.2: Three kinds of competition for the privacy tool. Direct. What it is: Does the same job the same way. At Sahaj: Tools like Rampart, and privacy features bundled with some cloud services. Indirect. What it is: Does the same job another way. At Sahaj: A person who reads each export before it goes out; a chat vendor whose software hides card numbers and nothing else. Status quo. What it is: What people do today, including nothing. At Sahaj: Farah's team blanking a number by hand when someone remembers, and a handbook line asking customers not to share sensitive details.
An export is a copy of data saved out of one system. A vendor is a company that sells you a service.

The status quo is usually the strongest rival. It is the old habit at home. It is free, it is familiar, and it partly works. A new product has to beat an afternoon in which nothing went wrong. Offices often mistake such afternoons for proof that all is well. So when someone says their product has no rivals, they usually have not looked at what people do now.

For each real alternative, Anaya made a competitor teardown. Think of two phones laid side by side on a table. She wrote down who each tool served, what it cost, what it did well, and what its customers complained about. The best place to find complaints was the reviews that users had left on public sites. What mattered was the complaint that kept coming back.
For these tools, three complaints kept coming back.
They worked well only in English. They flagged ordinary product codes and order numbers as if they were secrets. They were hard to set up over a weekend.
Saying where it fits.

The teardown gave her the material for one sentence. The sentence places the product among the other choices. It is called a positioning statement. It is like the line on a shop board that says who the shop is for and why it is different. Writing one takes discipline. A vague sentence is easy to write. A sharp one is hard.
Worked example: The guard's first positioning statement.

For companies that run customer chat in India and need to stop identity numbers travelling further than they should, the guard is a small privacy layer that understands English, Hindi and the two mixed. Unlike tools built for text in one writing system, it was made for the way people really type.
There is a test. Could the sentence describe a rival just as well? Then it is not a position yet. Anaya read hers aloud. She was glad that it fit none of the tools she had studied.
From conversations to ranked ideas.
It is tempting to jump from "I found a problem" to "I know what to build". That jump is how most unneeded software gets written. So Anaya put a drawing in between.

At the top of a page, she wrote the result she wanted: fewer personal details leave the chat. Below it she drew branches. Each branch was a need or a pain she had really heard. Beside each she wrote the numbers of the talks it came from.

The chatbot's greeting asks for details (conversations 2 and 3). Agents have no rule (1 and 5). Photographs are accepted without a second look (1). Numbers are typed in odd ways (4). Helpers type on behalf of people who do not know where the number goes (5).
Under each branch she listed a few ideas that might help.

This kind of drawing is an opportunity tree. It is like a family tree for ideas. It starts from the result you want. It branches into the needs people described. It ends in possible fixes. Anaya then ranked the branches with four questions. How many people did the need touch? How much did it hurt? How strong was the proof? Did it move the result at the top? She took care to rank by proof, not by excitement.

The tool she most wanted to build did not win. The greeting won. It had two conversations of proof, a free fix and a direct effect on the result. She wrote "rewrite the greeting this week" in the margin. She messaged Farah that afternoon.

The tool came second. It answered a different branch. Agents had no help, and nothing caught what the greeting missed. In the tree it sat under "no rule for agents". A line ran down to "a small tool that notices personal details and hides them".
Key idea: What the tree is for.
Think of the tree as a map of why. It shows when your favourite idea is only the second-best branch. It also records the reason. Each idea can be traced up to a need and down to proof.
Chapter summary.
A "yes, but" is a rule for the design. At Sahaj it fixed that the tool would run inside the company. That removed several designs at the start.

Check what already exists before you build. Test a rival's published claims yourself. Note where its reach ends. A bottom-up estimate counts customers you can name and multiplies by what each would pay. It marks every number as known or guessed. TAM, SAM and SOM shrink it from everyone with the problem to what you could win. Rivals are direct, indirect or the status quo. The status quo is usually the strongest. A teardown compares them and records the complaints that come back. A positioning statement says who the product is for and why it is different. It should not fit a rival equally well. An opportunity tree runs from result to need to idea. It ranks branches by proof. It shows when your favourite idea is not the best one.
Next, Anaya has to choose what to leave out. She cannot do everything on the tree.
